newsitem.title: JAPAN: FOCUS - Toyota says does not intend to curb exports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Toyota says does not intend to curb exports.

text.p: Japan's top carmaker, Toyota Motor Corp, said on Friday it had no intention of curbing its car exports to the United States, despite recent concerns over recurring U.S.-Japan trade friction.

"We've set up our (export) plans based on our supply-and-demand outlook and our U.S. exports this year will be up five percent year-on-year," Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda told a news conference in the central city of Nagoya. In calendar 1996, Toyota exported 433,000 cars to the United States.
A recent surge in Japan's car exports to the United States was a factor behind the rise in Japan's contentious trade surplus, often a source of bitter rows between the economic giants.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto heard concerns about the surplus from both the United States and Europe at last month's summit of the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations in Denver.
After the summit, U.S. President Bill Clinton said that Japan would risk an economic war with the United States if its trade surplus started exploding again.

On Wednesday, the Finance Ministry said Japan's current account surplus jumped 154.9 percent in May to 906.8 billion yen ($7.95 billion). The surplus in merchandise trade alone surged 118.6 percent from a year earlier to 927.9 billion yen ($8.14 billion).

The yen's recent weakness spurred Japanese car exports by making them cheaper abroad, but Toyota played down the possibility that currency rates would spark new trade tussles between Japan and the United States.
"The current levels are unlikely to cause such problems," the Toyota chief told reporters. The dollar was around 113.75 yen in Tokyo afternoon trade.
Okuda also said that a dollar/yen rate of between 110 yen and 120 yen was an appropriate level for the Japanese car industry, reiterating a statement he made earlier this week.
U.S. and Japanese automakers engaged in a war of words this week over the appropriate level for the dollar.

Earlier this week, Ford Motor Co vice-chairman Wayne Booker, who attended a meeting of the Japan-U.S. Business Council in San Francisco, said that a more appropriate dollar/yen rate would be in the range of 100 to 110 yen.
An executive from General Motors Co was also quoted as saying that the dollar should be around 105 yen.
Toyota's Okuda called Ford's view "too high for the yen".
